doc.title: Chuck Mancuso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 10, 2013

title: Mother's attitude on race and the black boy she walked to nursery school
summary: No musical tradition in the family; his mother insisted on treating black people decently, walked him and Buddy Clark to nursery school, and later became a pioneering woman manager.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Was there an Italian musical tradition in your family, in the circle?

No. I know. My mother married very big on race. Oh my God. You didn’t screw around with blacks. Because when I was in nursery school, she would take me to nursery school and the very next year my brother to nursery school, we were in a little housing thing. My father was off in World War II. And it was me, and this little other guy who was black, and my mother held my hand and his hand. And then two days a week the lady — right now I’m trying to remember the names, we were so close — would hold my hand and his hand and take us. And we got to be great friends throughout our lives, the kid and I.
A boy? A black boy also?

Yeah. We were both the same age. She would just go crazy. You know the Italians, the Italians and the Irish had this little separation and antagonism. They kind of hated each other, historically. If you read this recent book about 400 years of — a new book that just came out about Greenwich Village.

It’s a great book. And it talks about the animosity. There was always that kind of animosity. And there was something about some of my people that was tough about the blacks. You know, they used to call them melanzane you know? That was eggplant. Because it was a shiny black.
Wow. How do you spell that?

Melanzane — M-U-L — I don’t know. But my mother, oh my God, when she heard Grandpa Mancuso, a Sicilian tough guy, I don’t know, he had some light mob connections. He dealt the cards for the big games on Connecticut Street. She would rail at him. She says, “We don’t treat people like that,” you know, about blacks, if he ever said melanzane. So I came up —
But she didn’t want you to associate with black people —
She’s the one that walked me to school with the black kid.
Yeah, I’m talking kind of fast. Yeah, little Buddy Clark and Mrs. Clark. Some days Mrs. Clark would take myself and Buddy and the other days, and my mother, I have an award © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

in her name, she was the first female manager in New York State of the Unemployment Agency and Employment Agency both, in 1947, as a woman and as an Italian woman. She was a bright woman. So she was my model on how to deal with that stuff.
